clue.text: Quietly departed with the silver

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quietly
late can mean dead, departed this life

explanation.surface: Someone slipped away softly, taking the family silver with them.
explanation.definitionFit: Plate is the collective word for silverware and gilt dishes kept in a household.

clue.text: Dare he twist or stick?

indicators.note: to twist the words is to wring them into a new order

explanation.surface: A card player at blackjack deciding whether to take another card or stay.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is blackjack (pontoon), where players 'twist' for another card or 'stick'; here 'stick' is the definition, as a verb meaning cling.
explanation.definitionFit: To stick to something is to cling or be attached to it, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Not the best of the entries, usually

definitions.text: Not the best of the entries, usually

parts.words: Not the best of the entries, usually
parts.note: a way into a house at the rear, usually less grand than the front, and figuratively an underhand route in

explanation.definitionFit: A rear entrance to a building is rarely the finest way in, hence 'not the best'.

clue.text: A drink and a biscuit

definitions.meaning: an American whiskey distilled mainly from corn
a chocolate sandwich biscuit, a British teatime favourite

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a bourbon is also a familiar oblong chocolate biscuit with a chocolate cream filling.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a corn whiskey from Kentucky and a chocolate cream biscuit sold in Britain.

clue.text: Cast a spell with an appearance on stage

definitions.meaning: to bewitch or put into a trance, stressed on the second syllable
an actor's arrival in front of the audience

explanation.definitionFit: One spelling serves both the verb to bewitch and the noun for an actor coming on.

clue.text: Everyone in support of high-level operation shows courage

indicators.note: everyone is placed inside the support structure

parts.note: a gantry is an overhead framework supporting cranes, signals or rockets
all means everyone

explanation.surface: A team working high up on a scaffold display bravery.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallantry is bravery, especially in battle, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Ring-fighter pleased to be in the fresh air

parts.note: glad means pleased

indicators.note: the small word to must be in the middle of the reworked air
fresh suggests something newly made over, so the letters of air are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boxer happy to be outdoors, out of the stuffy gym.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' suggests a boxer, but a Roman arena fighter is meant; 'fresh' turns the letters into IAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A gladiator fought in the arena, the ring of a Roman amphitheatre.

clue.text: Sort of snake in the grass

definitions.text: Sort of snake in the grass

indicators.note: a sort of snake is the same letters sorted into another order

explanation.surface: A treacherous person, a hidden snake lurking in the grass.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'snake in the grass' is a treacherous person, and rearranging SNAKE gives a word for such a person, so the whole clue is both definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A snake in the grass is a hidden traitor, someone underhand and furtive.

clue.text: Inform against a place of business

definitions.meaning: British slang for betraying someone to the police
a store where goods are sold

explanation.definitionFit: The noun means a retail outlet, and as British slang the verb means betray someone to the police.

clue.text: Someone not suited for running

parts.note: not suited reads as wearing no clothes at all: a person who dashes naked across a pitch

explanation.definitionFit: A person who runs naked through a public place, often a sports ground, wears no suit at all.

clue.text: Novelist about fifty? Not quite

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, the novelist goes round fifty

parts.note: Thomas Hardy, the English novelist of Wessex
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Asks whether a writer is about fifty years old, and answers: not quite.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hardy wrote Tess of the d'Urbervilles; 'about' puts him around L.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardly means scarcely, barely, only just not.

clue.text: Brave man, he has heart of iron

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letters

explanation.surface: A courageous man with a heart of iron.
explanation.definitionFit: A hero is a person admired for courage, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Con-man?

parts.note: con read as against, as in pros and cons: a person who is against you

explanation.definitionFit: An adversary is a person against you, the 'con' side of pro and con.

clue.text: Legendary hero, led German line in WWII

definitions.meaning: the dragon-slaying hero of Germanic legend and Wagner's Ring
the name given to the German defensive line in the West, led as its first word

explanation.definitionFit: The Germanic legendary warrior gave his name to the defensive line Germany built along its western border.

clue.text: Odd sort of brazier

indicators.note: a sort of brazier is its letters sorted into a new order

explanation.surface: A strange kind of outdoor coal burner.
explanation.definitionFit: Bizarre means strange or weird, a synonym of odd.

clue.text: Particularly the highest

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means most importantly, and read literally means placed over everything.

clue.text: They enter the atmosphere from a remote point

indicators.note: from signals a word made out of the letters that follow

parts.note: taken as written
S, south, is a compass point

explanation.surface: Objects arriving into the air from somewhere far off in space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' signals a word made out of REMOTE, giving METEOR; S, a compass point, follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Shooting stars are bits of space debris burning up as they plunge into Earth's air.

clue.text: One always remembers the penal settlement

indicators.note: settlement suggests the letters being settled into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone who never forgets a convict colony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penal settlement' looks like a prison colony, but 'settlement' is the anagram signal on THE PENAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Proverbially this animal never forgets, so it is the one that always remembers.

clue.text: Needs developing, so tried a body-building drug

indicators.note: these letters need to be developed into a new form

explanation.surface: An athlete who tried a muscle-building drug and must now develop.
explanation.definitionFit: Anabolic steroids are synthetic hormones taken to build muscle mass.

clue.text: At sea no rating is lacking in knowledge

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A naval rank-and-file sailor afloat who knows nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rating' is a naval sailor below officer rank, which suits 'At sea', but here 'At sea' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignorant means uneducated or uninformed, without learning.

clue.text: Turning point in tax legislation

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A moment of change in the laws on taxation.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheel turns on this rod, literally a point about which something turns.

clue.text: This way for a place? You bet!

definitions.text: This way for a place? You bet!

parts.words: This way for a place? You bet!
parts.note: a horse-racing wager staked on a win and on a place, named with way

explanation.walkthrough: In British horse racing an 'each-way' bet backs a horse both to win and to finish in the places.
explanation.definitionFit: An each-way bet covers a horse winning or being placed, so this word with 'way' is the bet.

clue.text: Eats with the best

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means munches noisily, and the plural noun is short for champions.

clue.text: Advantage point in a number of games

indicators.note: the point goes inside the group of games

parts.note: a set in tennis is a number of games
S, south, is a compass point

explanation.surface: Winning a point during a run of tennis games gives an edge.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is a useful quality or benefit, something in your favour.

clue.text: Examination of French form included a severe test

indicators.note: the French word is included within the spoken exam

parts.note: an oral is a spoken examination
de is the French form of the English word of

explanation.surface: A spoken French exam proved a gruelling trial.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordeal is a painful or difficult experience, originally a trial by fire or water.

clue.text: Hold a show trial

parts.note: not a political prosecution but a try-out of a stage show before opening

explanation.definitionFit: Actors run through a play in practice before the premiere, giving the show a trial.

clue.text: He's almost all in but gets better

indicators.note: the shortened word goes inside he's

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive giving an S

indicators.note: almost means one letter short of the full word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone exhausted, nearly all in, but recovering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all in' is British for exhausted, but here 'in' is the container signal and 'almost' cuts the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To heal is to recover from injury or illness, become well.

clue.text: Billy tipped as a winner by Stevenson

parts.note: Billy the Kid, the American outlaw, or a billy goat's young
a nap is a racing tipster's best bet, so napped means tipped to win

explanation.surface: A racing tipster named Stevenson picks a horse called Billy to win.
explanation.walkthrough: In British racing a tipster's 'nap' is the day's surest selection; Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Louis Stevenson's adventure novel of David Balfour carries this title.
